# WHERE WE GROW NEXT
## International expansion: demand entry and supply entry as two separate decisions

**Board decision paper | v3.0 | 16 pages**
*Annex 1 (vendor-level detail, full research brief, draft Gate 0 SOWs) is available on request and is not required for this decision.*

---

### Changelog — what changed since v2.0 and why

| # | Change | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The "one hard rule" on origin (*"fibre and yarn may cross borders; fabric may not"*) is **withdrawn**. Replaced by a per-lane, per-HS-line origin matrix (§6.2) and named as a Gate 0 deliverable. | The withdrawn rule described one plausible reading of one regime (EVFTA) and was applied to three different duty lanes. It ignored cumulation, tolerance and direct-transport provisions, and would have caused us to reject qualifying options on the Vietnam→Japan lane. This was a technical error, not a simplification. |
| 2 | Corollary 1's FOB-vs-duty comparison replaced with a full landed-cost bridge on a common per-unit basis (§1.2). | The original compared percentages on different bases. |
| 3 | FX added as a first-class risk with a policy, not a footnote (§8.4). | JPY revenue against EUR/USD costs is plausibly the largest single P&L variable in this entry. It was absent from v2.0 entirely. |
| 4 | Japanese competitive set redrawn (§4.1). Claims of permanent incumbent ownership removed. | Uniqlo/Muji are the wrong primary threat. Domestic mid-premium and the secondhand/repair economy are. |
| 5 | Two-track independence downgraded from "one technical meeting point" to **five named coupling points with owners** (§2.3). | The tracks share working capital, attention, lead time and — most importantly — brand narrative. |
| 6 | Baseline financials restated from FY24 management accounts. `[R]` tags removed from internal data. | Internal figures are facts we hold, not quantities to research. |
| 7 | India organic fibre now carries an explicit chain-of-custody risk and a stated cost to the core (§6.4). | v2.0 violated its own §0.3 rule in its own executive summary. |
| 8 | Gate 0 broken into eight work packages with costs, a week-10 kill point, and named signatories per `[V]` item (§9). | A Board cannot approve an unbroken €290k line. |
| 9 | Decision sought narrowed from seven items to three, with four noted as provisional (§11). | Several v2.0 asks were for approval of things v2.0 said were untested. |
| 10 | Japan operational and compliance content added (§7). | The request is for positioning, channels **and initial operational steps**; v2.0 had none of the third. |

---

## The recommendation in short

Expansion into "a new region" is two decisions. **Demand entry** and **supply entry** have different criteria, different clock speeds, different failure modes and different owners. We propose:

- **Demand Track** — enter **Japan** as beachhead, selected on the scored criteria in §3.2, with **South Korea opened by trigger, not by date** (§3.5).
- **Supply Track** — qualify **Vietnam** as a new manufacturing origin, retaining **Portugal and Turkey** as nearshore replenishment, and treating **India as a certified organic fibre and yarn source only**, subject to the chain-of-custody controls in §6.4.

The tracks are **coupled at five points**, listed with owners in §2.3, of which the most consequential is brand narrative: a provenance brand entering Japan — an unusually origin-literate market with a live "Made in Japan" premium — carrying Vietnam-made goods. That is a positioning problem to be solved in §4.4, not a footnote.

Positioning is **not** "well-made sustainable basics." That segment is served at scale, cheaply, by incumbents with distribution we cannot match at this size. We enter as a **provable-longevity** brand — garments sold with their own evidence and their own repair pathway — at a price architecture defined in §4.3 that sits deliberately in the gap between mass-market and domestic heritage premium.

Channels are sequenced **credibility-first, capital-last**: agent/distributor and select wholesale before any entity, lease or local payroll (§5). Whether that sequence is *purchasable* at our current brand pull in Japan is itself an untested assumption and is Gate 0 work package WP4.

**Six load-bearing assumptions are named and untested** (§Annex A). Gate 0 exists to test them. §3.6 states in advance what results would flip the recommendation.

---

## §0 Scope, numbers, and the cost to the core

### 0.1 How to read the figures

Three kinds of number appear, tagged on first use.

| Tag | Type | Example | Achievable precision | Resolved by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[V]** | Verifiable fact | Tariff line, rule of origin, labelling statute, tax threshold | Binary — verify, never estimate | Gate 0, named counsel/broker (§9.3) |
| **[R]** | Researchable quantity | Import volumes, competitor retail prices, wholesale margin norms, CAC | Trade/customs data ±15%. **Niche premium segment sizing: ±40% at best** | Gate 0, field research |
| **[D]** | Design target | Our Year-3 revenue, channel mix, vendor count, price points | A choice, not a discovery | Gate 1, by this Board |

**On the ±40%.** We should be explicit about what that precision can and cannot support. It cannot support a revenue forecast. It *can* support a go/no-go, provided the decision is framed as: **is the low bound of the segment estimate still above the break-even volume?** §9.4 sets that test numerically. If we find ourselves needing the mid-point estimate to justify entry, the answer is no.

Everything touching tariff preference, rules of origin, labelling, green claims or entity law is **[V]** — a Gate 0 verification item, not a settled fact in this paper. Preference regimes phase down, graduate and expire; §6.5 prices that risk.

### 0.2 In scope / out of scope

| In scope | Out of scope |
|---|---|
| One new demand region, entered through one beachhead country | Wholesale expansion inside existing EU markets |
| One new manufacturing origin, plus fibre sourcing | Renegotiating existing Portuguese/Turkish terms |
| Substantiation infrastructure (required by EU Green Claims/ESPR regardless) | M&A, licensing, franchising |
| Market-fit adaptation, defined as: JIS size re-grading, Japanese-language labelling and content, colourway and fit adjustment, seasonal calendar shift | Category extension beyond that definition |
| FX exposure arising from JPY-denominated revenue | Group-level treasury policy |
| The organisational capacity to run both tracks without degrading the core | — |

### 0.3 The rule of this document

**Every commitment to the new market carries a stated cost to the core business** — attention, working capital, or inventory risk. This is enforced numerically in §2.4 (attention budget) and §8.3 (working-capital draw), and each major line in §§4–7 carries a cost-to-core column. A line item without a named cost has not been thought through, and in v2.0 at least one such line survived into the executive summary.

### 0.4 Baseline (FY24 management accounts, unaudited where noted)

| Metric | FY24 |
|---|---|
| Revenue | €78.4m |
| Gross margin | 57.9% |
| EBITDA | 8.5% (€6.7m) |
| Headcount | 214 FTE |
| DE / NL / Nordics share of revenue | 62% |
| Wholesale / DTC split | 55 / 45 |
| Net working capital | €21.3m (99 days) |
| Committed facility headroom | €6.0m undrawn |
| Inventory | €14.9m, 141 days |

These are our own numbers. They are not bracketed and not tagged.

---

## §1 The three questions, and the landed-cost bridge

### 1.1 Framing

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| Which country next? | What are we short of — customers, margin, capacity, or credibility — and which geography is the cheapest source of *that specific thing*? |
| Where can we sell sustainable clothing? | Where is sustainability a **purchase driver** rather than a **tiebreaker**? |
| Where can we manufacture more cheaply? | What is our **landed cost after duty, freight, inventory carry, defect rate, compliance overhead and FX** — and does preference actually apply to *our* bill of materials, on *this* lane? |

### 1.2 Corollary 1 — the landed-cost bridge

v2.0 asserted that a 15% FOB saving is "erased" by an 11.5% duty. That compared percentages on different bases and mixed the EU and Japan lanes. Corrected, on a common per-unit basis, for a representative core knit style (HS 6109/6110 class), **all figures [D] modelling assumptions pending WP1/WP5 verification**:

| Cost element | Portugal (current) | Vietnam (modelled) | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| FOB / EXW per unit | €18.60 | €14.80 | −20.4% FOB |
| Freight + insurance to EU DC | €0.35 (road) | €1.05 (sea LCL equiv.) | |
| **Customs value (CIF basis)** | €18.95 | €15.85 | Both EU and Japan assess duty on CIF **[V]** |
| Duty — EU lane, preference granted | €0.00 (EU internal) | €0.00 (EVFTA) | |
| Duty — EU lane, **preference fails** | n/a | €1.90 (12% MFN, EU) **[V]** | EU MFN for most HS61/62 lines |
| Inventory carry on lead-time delta | €0.00 | €0.62 | +65 days at 8% cost of capital on CIF |
| Defect/rework provision | €0.19 (1.0%) | €0.48 (2.5%, year 1) | Falls to ~1.4% by year 3 if vendor performs |
| Audit, testing, compliance amortised | €0.08 | €0.34 | New-origin due diligence, CoC, testing |
| Origin documentation & broker | €0.02 | €0.11 | |
| **Landed cost, preference granted** | **€19.24** | **€18.40** | **−4.4%** |
| **Landed cost, preference fails** | **€19.24** | **€20.30** | **+5.5% — worse than staying** |

**The point survives the correction, but with a different shape.** A 20% FOB saving becomes a 4.4% landed saving when preference holds, and a 5.5% landed *penalty* when it does not. The swing factor is not labour cost; it is **origin qualification**, which is why §6.2 is the most important technical section in this paper.

*This bridge is EU-lane. The Japan lane is separate and is modelled in §6.3. Japan's apparel MFN rates are materially lower than the EU's — indicatively in the 7–11% band depending on HS line **[V]** — and Japan already extends preference to Vietnam under multiple agreements, so the Japan-lane downside of origin failure is smaller. Quoting an EU rate in a Japan paper without labelling the lane is exactly the confusion §0.1 exists to prevent, and v2.0 committed it.*

### 1.3 Corollary 2 — the second-cheapest thing is usually the expensive one

Of the four things we might be short of, only two are geography-solvable at our size: **new customer segments** (Demand Track) and **capacity at acceptable landed cost** (Supply Track). Credibility is earned in-market, not imported. Margin is a consequence, not a destination.

---

## §2 The two-track structure

### 2.1 Why separate

| | Demand Track | Supply Track |
|---|---|---|
| Objective | Access a customer segment that pays for longevity | Capacity + landed cost + risk diversification |
| Clock | 24–36 months to meaningful contribution | 9–15 months to first qualified PO |
| Failure mode | Slow burn: inventory ages, channel partner disengages | Fast and expensive: defects, origin failure, audit finding |
| Reversibility | High if asset-light (contracts, not leases) | Medium — sunk qualification cost, retained dual-sourcing |
| Owner | CCO | COO |
| Primary metric | Full-price sell-through by channel | Landed cost after risk; on-time-in-full |

Fusing them produces the classic mid-size error: manufacturing where you sell, because it feels coherent. Coherence is not a criterion.

### 2.2 What we are *not* claiming

v2.0 claimed the tracks meet at one technical point. That was wrong.

### 2.3 The five coupling points, with owners

| # | Coupling | Nature | Owner | Control |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | **Origin & duty** | Vietnam sourcing changes the duty position on both the EU lane and any Japan lane | COO + Head of Trade Compliance | §6.2 origin matrix; per-HS decision, not per-brand |
| C2 | **Working capital** | Both tracks draw the same €6.0m facility headroom | CFO | §8.3 combined draw ceiling of €4.2m; hard stop |
